audits.claim: Exact use of the Golden Urn in individual successions remains (to-verify) against case evidence and Oidtmann (2018), not only the 2011 institutional statement.
audits.source_locator: Oidtmann 2014 Harvard PhD dissertation (precursor of the 2018 book), printed p. 22 (PDF p. 38); also printed pp. 14, 21, 131-132, 176-177, 184-185 (PDF pp. 30, 37, 147-148, 192-193, 200-201); printed page = PDF page - 16 for body pages
audits.source_excerpt: In practice, the statute was generally applied to those lineages of reincarnate lamas who had been enrolled in the registers of the Lifanyuan and were eligible to receive the title of kūtuktu when they turned eighteen.
audits.retrieval_method: Harvard DASH DSpace REST discovery, then curl download of the repository bitstream Oidtmann_gsas.harvard_0084L_11276.pdf (26916873 bytes, sha256 1b7b9800575e33dd50bc861ff331a2a59a12d5eb7684a57ee02634bc6343c9ec); pdftotext extraction; quotes read verbatim from the extraction. Stable alternative in the document itself: http://nrs.harvard.edu/urn-3:HUL.InstRepos:11745702. Scratch copy under reports/supplement-opencode-1/scratch/round5-06/.
audits.basis: Partial support, stated exactly: the retrieved case evidence supports the entry's claim that exact use must be read against case evidence beyond the 2011 statement, and it now supplies that case layer - but it does not settle the individual ninth-to-twelfth Dalai Lama successions. Statutory scope was broader than practice: the Lifanyuan statute applied to "the Dalai Lama, Panchen [Lama] and all other reincarnations" (printed p. 22), yet "in practice" covered Lifanyuan-enrolled kutuktu-eligible lineages (featured excerpt). First uses were the 1793 trial runs identifying five lineages (Sumpa Kutuktu plus four Khorchin), where "the court intended the Golden Urn to supersede not only the oracles but also the divination authority of the Dalai Lama and Panchen Lama" (printed pp. 131-132). The Eighth Dalai Lama's own 1793 decree broadened the ritual to "all reincarnations of lamas born in the land of Tibet" while keeping oracles "in the nomination of candidates for the final Golden Urn lottery" (printed pp. 176-177): an emic articulation diverging from Qing internal plans. Oidtmann argues contemporaries understood the urn "not as a randomized 'lottery' but rather as a divination ritual" (printed p. 14), and that exemptions were negotiated case by case while the court insisted on the urn for major lineages (printed pp. 184-185). This vindicates the entry's distinction between the 2011 emic statement and archival case evidence.
audits.coupling_implication: Era/institution/naming coupling: the urn is a late-eighteenth-century statutory technology whose application to any given succession was negotiated, ritually framed, and enrollment-dependent; recognition, appointment, and state approval remain distinct acts (entry section 8 "Actors differ"). A fictional state-recognition protocol must store per-case use and the drawing's understood meaning, not a standing universal randomizer.
audits.limits: The retrieved text is the 2014 dissertation, not the 2018 book; its Amdo-centered cases do not directly document the 1815-1875 Dalai Lama successions, so the 2011 statement's "only the Eleventh and Twelfth" claim is neither confirmed nor contradicted here, and downstream (to-verify) markers should remain. Goldstein's "every effort was made to circumvent its use" appears only as a cited footnote (printed p. 195), not as Oidtmann's own conclusion. The New Books Network episode summary (newbooksnetwork.com/max-oidtmann-forging-the-golden-urn-the-qing-empire-and-the-politics-of-reincarnation-in-tibet-columbia-up-2018, 2019) was also retrieved but is the host's paraphrase, not case evidence. No living religious or political authority is adjudicated.

audits.claim: Recognition-history correction: Gamble emphasizes the Third Karmapa, Rangjung Dorje (1284-1339), and the institutionalization of multi-life narrative.

audits.basis: Gamble's own text - not a publisher abstract - states the argument the entry attributes to her. Identity and dates: "Rang byung rdo rje (1284-1339)" and "Rang byung rdo rje, the third Karmapa" (PDF p. 12). Thesis subject: his influence on religious institutions, "particularly the religious institution of reincarnation" (PDF p. 26). Recognition history: the First Karmapa was "only posthumously recognised as a Karmapa" (featured excerpt, PDF p. 20), and Rangjung's recognition as his reincarnation included him "within a conception of personal time that was virtually infinite" built on the two predecessors' groundwork (PDF p. 20) - retrospective numbering and gradual institutionalization, matching the entry's correction. The introduction connects his sacred-site and literary projects to the development of Tibet's first reincarnation lineages (PDF p. 6), and reports that a predecessor told Rangjung's multi-life story using Indian jataka birth-story elements (PDF p. 53; OCR-spaced in extraction, so paraphrased). Supported as whole-claim confirmation at the level of the thesis text: Third Karmapa emphasis, retrospective recognition, and multi-life narrative as constructed, institutionally developing tradition.
audits.coupling_implication: Language/myth/era coupling: recognition vocabulary and lineage numbering are retrospective; the multi-life narrative is a literary construction with Indic (jataka) sources; institutionalization is tied to specific thirteenth-fourteenth-century actors, sites, and patrons. Fictional lineages should date their own recognition practices and not put later titles in the first figure's lifetime mouth (entry section 8 "Numbering is retrospective").
audits.limits: The retrieved text is the 2014 doctoral thesis, the argument's earlier version; the 2018 Oxford book itself remains unverified, and the prior ledger's publisher-abstract check (403-blocked) stays unreproduced - the entry's register row still cites the book. Thesis extraction has OCR spacing artifacts; quoted strings above are verbatim clean segments and mangled phrases are paraphrased. Gamble's first-lineage framing concerns Karmapa history, not a pan-Tibetan census of earlier succession practices. No living claimant, lineage dispute, or religious/political authority is adjudicated.
